newsitem.title: UK: Queen Elizabeth has 8,000 to golden wedding party.
newsitem.headline: Queen Elizabeth has 8,000 to golden wedding party.

text.p: Britain's Queen Elizabeth threw open her garden gates on Tuesday to welcome 4,000 couples who share with her the increasingly rare achievement of a marriage that has lasted for 50 years.
The queen and her husband Prince Philip invited couples from as far away as Australia who married, as they did, in 1947, to a special Golden Wedding garden party at Buckingham Palace.
Smiling guests poured out of the palace, after enjoying cakes, sandwiches, tea and iced coffee in the royal marquee, accompanied by brass band music and unusually sunny weather.
"It was wonderful, a really fantastic day. Something to remember for ever," said Dee Reid, one of just 15 couples invited from New Zealand.
She had saved one of the yellow cakes decorated with the initials ER and the number 50.

Decked in colourful outfits, with hats for the ladies and morning suits for the gentlemen obligatory, a few of the guests exchanged brief words with the royal couple as they walked along a pathway through the crowd.

"I told her I still had a little commemorative bottle of whisky from years ago, and she answered 'Have you really? You mean you've not opened it?'," said 82-year-old Frederic Rays from Kent, south England.
"She was really chatty, such a nice person."
The queen wore a bright lemon dress and matching pill-box hat, with mushroom-coloured gloves.
Prince Philip, dressed in a pale grey suit with panama hat, chatted to a number of ex-naval officers amongst the guests.
"I shook his hand," said a lady from Essex, whose husband swapped war stories with the duke. "I won't wash it for weeks."
The pair made their way to the royal tent, where a privileged few guests who share their November 20 wedding date were invited to eat refreshments with them.
Salmon and cucumber sandwiches, strawberry tarts and ice cream were among the delicacies.
But guests said getting food was chaotic. "It was a real bunfight," said one.

Couples who responded to newspaper advertisements inviting them to apply for invitations flew to Britain from Commonwealth countries for the occasion - one of numerous events planned to mark the royal wedding anniversary in November.

Nearly 600 couples from Australia applied but only 50 were granted invitations in the palace's random selection. They went to the Australian embassy in London on Tuesday to collect the coveted invitations.
"They were so excited they got here 40 minutes early," said Jane Byford, a spokeswoman at Australia House, as she lined the couples up to have commemorative photographs taken.
"It's something you wouldn't even dream about," said Dutch-born Ricky Kroon, who says her husband fell in love with her over half a century ago when he saw her coming out of a stable cuddling a lamb.

Royal garden parties have been held since the 1860s. The three that take place in London every summer are normally attended by about 8,000 people, many from government, the civil service and the armed forces.
For Britons, the golden wedding celebrations are a reminder of a now distant era when the royals were the nation's first family, setting a moral benchmark for their subjects to follow.
The image was shattered by the bitter and highly public breakdown of heir-to-the-throne Prince Charles' marriage to Princess Diana and the confessions of both that they had affairs.
All three of the queen's four children who married later divorced. Her youngest son Prince Edward is still single, while her daughter Princess Anne has remarried.
